textTitles: The catalogue of everything that grows

texts.title: The catalogue of everything that grows

paragraphs.text: A seed bank looks like a library and behaves like one, which is the best way to understand what it is for. Its holdings are not specimens to be admired but copies to be lent: a plant breeder writes in, describes a problem — a disease, a drought, a soil too salty for the local variety — and receives a small packet of seed that may contain the resistance nobody has needed until now. The world has around seventeen hundred such collections, holding several million samples between them.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The reason they exist is a narrowing that happened quickly. Through the twentieth century, farmers across the world replaced local varieties with a much smaller number of high-yielding ones, and the replaced varieties disappeared from fields within a generation of being abandoned. The gain in yield was enormous and is not seriously disputed; the cost was that the genetic material accumulated by several thousand years of selection stopped being maintained by the people who had maintained it, and had to be kept somewhere else or not at all.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Keeping seed alive is more demanding than storing it. Most crop seeds can be dried and frozen and will survive for decades at minus twenty degrees, but they do not survive indefinitely, and a collection must periodically take a sample out, grow it, and harvest fresh seed. That process, called regeneration, is where the work and the risk are: a sample grown in the wrong conditions, pollinated by a neighbouring plot or harvested from too few individuals comes back to the store subtly different from what went in.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Some crops cannot be frozen at all. Potatoes, bananas, cassava and most fruit trees either produce no viable seed or produce seed that does not survive drying, so they are kept as living plants in fields or as tissue cultures in jars that must be transferred to fresh medium several times a year. These collections cost far more per sample than a freezer, are exposed to storms, disease and budget cuts, and hold exactly the crops on which the most people depend for calories.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The system is duplicated on purpose. National collections deposit copies with international ones, and a facility inside a mountain in the Arctic holds backup copies for depositors who retain ownership of what they send. The facility has been used in the way it was designed to be used: a regional collection destroyed in a war withdrew its deposit, regenerated the seed elsewhere and sent fresh copies back. That single episode is the clearest demonstration that the redundancy is not theatre.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Access is governed by agreements that took decades to negotiate. A plant’s genetic material has value, and the countries where crop diversity is richest are generally not the countries with the largest seed industries, which made the question of who may use what, and on what terms, a long argument. The treaty that resulted creates a pool of crops that can be exchanged freely for research and breeding, with a share of commercial benefit returning to a common fund. Whether enough returns is disputed by everyone involved.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Banks are not the only form of conservation and are not the best one on their own. A variety kept in a freezer stops evolving on the day it is deposited, while the pests and the climate it was bred against do not; a variety still grown in a field continues to adapt. Conservation in the field is therefore not a picturesque alternative to the bank but a complement to it, and the programmes that work pay farmers to keep growing what is otherwise uncompetitive.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: What the collections are for becomes obvious in a crisis and invisible the rest of the time. A wheat disease that appeared in East Africa in the late 1990s was eventually countered with resistance found in old material held in collections, and the breeding that followed took more than a decade. The lesson is about timing rather than heroism: the material has to be in store, catalogued and alive before anyone knows which sample will matter, and that work is funded by nobody in particular during the years when nothing is going wrong. A collection is therefore judged in the one season it is needed and neglected in the forty before it, which is a poor arrangement and the one every country has.
paragraphs.label: H
